title: Formic-acid treatment of timothy-grass liquid fraction: dose and precipitation pH reference
publication: Grassland Science in Europe, Volume 29, Why grasslands?, pp. 128–130
license_status: No explicit reuse license identified in the proceedings PDF; assess permission before commercial redistribution.
source_location: Article: Table 1 and Materials and methods, pp. 128–130

experimental_context.feedstock: Pure timothy grass (Phleum pratense), second cut harvested 31 July 2023, Jokioinen, Finland
experimental_context.press: Pilot-scale single-screw press; liquid yield reported as 27.5% of fresh matter
experimental_context.precipitation: Formic acid addition followed by natural sedimentation in 500 ml bottles for up to 21 days; three replicates per treatment

dose_basis_check: The proceedings report 4–10 L/Mg, while its methods report 0.2–0.5 ml pure formic acid added to 500 g liquid. Using 1 Mg = 1000 kg, these bottle amounts calculate to 0.4–1.0 L/t, tenfold lower than the stated treatment labels. Both source representations are preserved; the discrepancy is unresolved and the dose is not suitable for reagent-demand activation.
calculation_method: bottle dose (ml) / liquid mass (kg) gives ml/kg; numerically this equals L/t because 1 ml/kg = 1 L/t. Arithmetic normalization only; not a measured or corrected dose.
reported_pH: Brown-liquid pH means by treatment are transcribed from Table 1; SEM 0.01, p-values as printed.
response_table_data: The four Table 1 treatment-response rows (dry matter, ash, crude protein and true protein) are transcribed verbatim in the companion grass_liquid_formic_acid_table1_response_stefanski_2024_reference.csv. The printed 'g kg fresh liquid^-1' denominator conflicts with the article's sediment mass/component hierarchy, so these values are quarantined and not interpreted or used in calculations until the source basis is clarified.
limitations: Timothy grass and Finnish pilot-scale liquid fraction are not GreenHub roadside-grass juice.

An apparent tenfold discrepancy exists between the reported L/Mg labels and per-bottle acid amount; do not use these doses as a model parameter or TEA consumption rate until verified against authors or a corrected source.
The experiment used natural sedimentation, not GreenHub's isoelectric precipitation and centrifugation route.
The conference proceeding has no DOI or explicit license identified in the accessed PDF; redistribution rights require review.
